extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing examiner guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre‑AIA 112, first paragraph). Focuses on how examiners should read the disclosure, construct claims, identify unsupported claim limitations, and make a prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement compels disclosure of the technologic knowledge upon which the patent is based and demonstrates that the patentee (inventor) was in possession of the invention that is claimed; it promotes the progress of the useful arts by ensuring adequate description in exchange for the right to exclude others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains policy rationale for the requirement and anchors subsequent analysis — the specification must adequately describe the invention in return for the patent monopoly (Capon v. Eshhar and related authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency standard — possession by one skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy the written description requirement, a patent specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance is a fact‑based inquiry that varies with the nature of the invention; cites cases such as Moba v. Diamond, Vas‑Cath, Enzo Biochem. The examiner must determine whether the disclosure conveys reasonable clarity that inventor was in possession as of the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of disclosure that can show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas that fully set forth the claimed invention, including description of all claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists multiple descriptive means and cites Lockwood; possession may be established by actual reduction to practice, drawings, structural chemical formulas, or distinguishing identifying characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice or "ready for patenting"
rubrics_metrics.description: A showing of possession may be shown by an actual reduction to practice or by showing the invention was 'ready for patenting' (e.g., disclosure of drawings or structural chemical formulas that show the invention was complete).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and citations (Pfaff, Eli Lilly, Amgen). Reduction to practice may be shown by constructing an embodiment or performing a process that meets all claim limitations and shows it works for its intended purpose; testing may be required depending on the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposits of biological materials as support (but not a substitute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to a deposit of biological material may satisfy the written description requirement for claimed biological materials, but a deposit is not a substitute for a written description; the written description of the deposited material should be as complete as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Enzo Biochem and the Deposit of Biological Materials rule (37 CFR 1.801 et seq.; 54 Fed. Reg. 34,864). Explains that deposits aid verification and infringement questions; deposits made after filing can support corrections only with required statements under 37 CFR 1.804.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of adequacy for original claims and examiner's initial burden
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; the examiner has the initial burden, after a thorough reading, to present evidence or reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as providing adequate support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Wertheim. To make a prima facie case, the examiner must identify the specific claim limitations not adequately supported and explain why the claim is not fully supported by the disclosure (Hyatt v. Dudas example). If applicant points to support, burden shifts back to examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claims — essential/critical feature requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention as a whole may not be adequately described if the claims require an essential or critical feature that is not adequately described in the specification and which is not conventional or known in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples (e.g., gene claim including promoters or regulatory elements not described). If specification indicates a particular feature is essential, omitting it in a claim can render the claim unsupported (Gentry Gallery, Tronzo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method/function descriptions vs. structure (structure‑function correlation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention described solely in terms of a method of making and/or its function may lack written descriptive support where there is no described or art‑recognized correlation between the disclosed function and the structures responsible for the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: amino acid sequence plus genetic code may support a genus of nucleic acids but not naturally occurring DNA/mRNA; the mere fact a product would be obvious from a process does not satisfy written description (In re Bell, In re Deuel, Eli Lilly/Fonar distinction for software).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere obviousness is insufficient for written description
rubrics_metrics.description: A description that merely renders the claimed invention obvious may not sufficiently describe the invention for purposes of the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Eli Lilly and contrasts with situations where functional disclosure of software may be adequate due to skill in the art (Fonar). Examiner should not conflate obviousness with possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: New or amended claims — prohibition on new matter and support requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: New or amended claims must be supported by the original disclosure; the proscription against introduction of new matter (35 U.S.C. 132 and 251) prevents adding subject matter beyond what was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Rasmussen and related cases. Newly added claims or limitations must be supported by express, implicit, or inherent disclosure. If original claims disclose material not elsewhere in the specification, applicant may amend the specification to include it (In re Benno), but the reverse is not permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections and permissible amendments (obvious error and sequencing errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to correct an obvious error do not constitute new matter where the ordinary artisan would recognize the error and the appropriate correction; corrections of sequence errors may be permissible where they conform to deposited material and applicable rules are followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Oda and sequencing error literature; discusses Cubist v. Hospira where correction of sequence information was allowed when the specification disclosed identifying characteristics and a deposit was referenced; deposits made after filing can be relied on for corrections only with a statement under 37 CFR 1.804.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of a limitation may indicate lack of possession of broader genus
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of a limitation in a claim can raise an issue whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention; claims that omit matter described as essential in the specification do not comply with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: PIN/NIP, Gentry Gallery, Johnson Worldwide, Tronzo. If the specification makes clear a narrow understanding is essential, broader claims may be unsupported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner methodology — read and analyze the specification first
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should thoroughly read and evaluate the entire content of the application when reviewing for compliance with the written description requirement, recognizing the presumption of adequacy and then presenting reasons to overcome it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes that the examiner must identify unsupported limitations and explain deficiency; suggests what may constitute a sufficient examiner statement (e.g., 'applicant has not pointed out where the new (or amended) claim is supported'). Citations include MPEP § 2163.04 and Hyatt v. Dudas.

rubrics_metrics.name: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers (claim construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction is essential: each claim must be separately analyzed and given a reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description; the entire claim (including preamble and transitional phrase) must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Katz, In re Morris, and other authorities. The examiner should determine the scope and meaning of the claim, including weight to give the preamble and meaning of transitional terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrases and preamble treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand and apply the meaning of transitional phrases ('comprising', 'consisting essentially of', 'consisting of') and evaluate whether preamble language constitutes a structural limitation; the claim as a whole must be supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains 'comprising' is open‑ended; 'consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground and should be construed relative to the specification; applicant bears burden to show additional elements do not materially change basic and novel properties. Citations: Genentech v. Chiron, PPG, AK Steel, Janakirama‑Rao.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the entire application for support of each element/step
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to determining adequacy, the examiner should review the claims and entire specification (specific embodiments, figures, sequence listings) to understand how applicant provides support for each claimed feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that disclosure of an element may be critical and must be compared to the scope of the claim from viewpoint of one skilled in the art; cites Rasmussen and Amgen examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of level of ordinary skill and known information
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis should be conducted from the standpoint of one of ordinary skill in the art at the filing date; information well known in the art need not be described in detail, and there may be an inverse correlation between level of skill and specificity required in the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Wang Labs, Hybritech. Examiners should determine the field of the invention and the relevant skill level, which affects how much detail is necessary to show possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency may be shown by drawings, formulae, or identifying characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate written description may be shown by detailed drawings, structural or generic chemical formulas, generic formulae for a genus, or other identifying characteristics that permit a skilled person to recognize inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites cases where drawings alone provided written description (Vas‑Cath, Wolfensperger) and discusses generic chemical formulae as normally adequate descriptions of claimed genera (Eli Lilly). The description need only detail what is new or not conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function plus minimal structure can suffice when correlation exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description may be satisfied through disclosure of function and minimal structure when there is a well‑established correlation between structure and function such that one skilled in the art can predict structure from function with reasonable confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Enzo Biochem and the Written Description Guidelines example. This is particularly relevant in arts where structure‑function correlations are established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural standard for making a prima facie case and burden shifting
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a prima facie case of inadequate written description, the examiner must identify unsupported claim limitations and explain why the claim is not supported; a clear explanation can shift the burden to applicant to point to support or amend claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyatt v. Dudas example: examiner explicitly explained why combination of elements lacked adequate support; for amended claims, a simple statement that applicant hasn't pointed out support may suffice where support is not apparent. See MPEP §§ 2163.04, 714.02, 2163.06.
